questions.q: The editorial names two things that make a person modest. Which?
options: A scientific bent of mind and the fear of God
Yes. Each makes one see oneself against something far greater.
Poverty and old age
Not quite. The article says: A scientific bent of mind and the fear of God.
Criticism and failure
Not quite. The article says: A scientific bent of mind and the fear of God.
Silence and solitude
Not quite. The article says: A scientific bent of mind and the fear of God.
questions.rationale: “There are two things in this world which make a person modest. One is a scientific bent of mind; the other is being God-fearing.”

questions.q: How does a truly scientific mind escape pride, according to the editorial?
options: It studies only small subjects
Not quite. The article says: It measures itself against the vastness of knowledge, not against less accomplished people.
It avoids the company of others
Not quite. The article says: It measures itself against the vastness of knowledge, not against less accomplished people.
It measures itself against the vastness of knowledge, not against less accomplished people
Well reasoned. Before knowledge, everyone is small.
It never speaks of its achievements
Not quite. The article says: It measures itself against the vastness of knowledge, not against less accomplished people.
questions.rationale: “In relation to the person who has knowledge, one can think of oneself as greater than others but in relation to the vast world of knowledge, everyone is less in stature.”

questions.q: Father Heras could have taught the European history he knew. What does his choice of an unfamiliar subject show, in the article’s view?
options: One with a purpose chooses what serves the goal and accepts the labour it costs
Right. Not what is easiest or best paid.
He wanted a higher salary
Not quite. The article says: One with a purpose chooses what serves the goal and accepts the labour it costs.
He disliked European history
Not quite. The article says: One with a purpose chooses what serves the goal and accepts the labour it costs.
He was told there was no other vacancy
Not quite. The article says: One with a purpose chooses what serves the goal and accepts the labour it costs.
questions.rationale: “If one has a purpose in life, then one will overlook all other considerations and concentrate on achieving one’s goal.”

questions.article: A Happy Ending to the Tragedy of Life
questions.q: Seeing the newly built capital at the close of British rule, a visitor remarked, “What a magnificent world they built to leave.” How does the article apply this to everyone?
options: Great cities never last
Not quite. The article says: We each build a world here and must leave it; only the Hereafter gives the story a happy ending.
One should not build at all
Not quite. The article says: We each build a world here and must leave it; only the Hereafter gives the story a happy ending.
Builders are seldom thanked
Not quite. The article says: We each build a world here and must leave it; only the Hereafter gives the story a happy ending.
We each build a world here and must leave it; only the Hereafter gives the story a happy ending
Yes. Without it, life is a tragedy.
questions.rationale: “Life is a tragedy when seen without the Hereafter. This tragedy can only be given a happy ending with the addition of the life to come.”

questions.q: What simple formula does the article credit to Sir Syed Ahmad Khan?
options: Solve every problem before starting work
Not quite. The article says: Ignore the problems and avail of the opportunities.
Wait until conditions are ideal
Not quite. The article says: Ignore the problems and avail of the opportunities.
Ignore the problems and avail of the opportunities
Correct. Problems and opportunities exist side by side.
Protest until grievances are heard
Not quite. The article says: Ignore the problems and avail of the opportunities.
questions.rationale: “He gave the people a viable formula: Ignore the problems, feed the opportunities, and, by availing of opportunities, build your life.”

questions.q: Why, according to the article, are reformers so often opposed in their own time and praised later?
options: Because people dislike the educated
Not quite. The article says: Contemporaries cannot foresee the results of their guidance; later generations can see them.
Contemporaries cannot foresee the results of their guidance; later generations can see them
Well read. Foresight is rare; hindsight is easy.
Because reformers seek opposition
Not quite. The article says: Contemporaries cannot foresee the results of their guidance; later generations can see them.
Because reformers are usually rude
Not quite. The article says: Contemporaries cannot foresee the results of their guidance; later generations can see them.
questions.rationale: “Those who nowadays extol his virtues, do so in retrospect, having had the opportunity to see the results of his guidance, whereas his own contemporaries were so lacking in foresight.”

questions.q: Several large efforts to build a good society disappointed. What does the article call the basic shortcoming?
options: The wrong laws were passed
Not quite. The article says: Thinking only in terms of systems, instead of reforming individuals – the building blocks of society.
There were too few leaders
Not quite. The article says: Thinking only in terms of systems, instead of reforming individuals – the building blocks of society.
Thinking only in terms of systems, instead of reforming individuals – the building blocks of society
Right. Reform individuals and society follows.
Too little money was spent
Not quite. The article says: Thinking only in terms of systems, instead of reforming individuals – the building blocks of society.
questions.rationale: “Our basic shortcoming is to think purely in terms of systems… The individual is the primary unit of society. If individuals are reformed, society follows suit.”

questions.q: What spirit does the article require for a dialogue between communities to succeed?
options: Claim and counter-claim until one side yields
Not quite. The article says: Reconciliation, not rivalry – ready to give as well as take, with the result in mind.
Settling who was at fault in the past
Not quite. The article says: Reconciliation, not rivalry – ready to give as well as take, with the result in mind.
Reconciliation, not rivalry – ready to give as well as take, with the result in mind
Yes. “A brotherly meeting,” not a contest.
Each side defending its prestige
Not quite. The article says: Reconciliation, not rivalry – ready to give as well as take, with the result in mind.
questions.rationale: “The feeling at work behind dialogue is one of reconciliation and not of rivalry… while taking from others they will also be willing to give.”

questions.q: How does the article describe the opening chapter of the Quran in relation to the rest?
options: A miniature picture of the believer, of which the rest of the Quran is the enlargement
Exactly. Gratitude, submission and a plea for guidance.
A list of the chapters to follow
Not quite. The article says: A miniature picture of the believer, of which the rest of the Quran is the enlargement.
A historical introduction
Not quite. The article says: A miniature picture of the believer, of which the rest of the Quran is the enlargement.
A prayer unconnected with what follows
Not quite. The article says: A miniature picture of the believer, of which the rest of the Quran is the enlargement.
questions.rationale: “The opening chapter of the Quran is a miniature picture of such a believer, and the rest of the Quran an enlargement of this picture.”

questions.q: In this world a person’s words are weighed by his wealth and following. What, says the commentary, will carry weight on the Day of Judgement?
options: The number of one’s supporters
Not quite. The article says: Truth alone.
The grandeur of one’s position
Not quite. The article says: Truth alone.
The eloquence of one’s speech
Not quite. The article says: Truth alone.
Truth alone
Well read. Falsehood will be left without arguments.
questions.rationale: “Truth alone will be of weight that Day… all the weight will be on the side of the Truth: Falsehood will be divested of all its arguments.”
